Living On Cheese

By: Kate Barry | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Welcome to Centurion - where a water leak is not just a water leak - it literally dissolves the ground beneath your feet.

Unique Selling Point:
Lourensa takes us on a topless party bus Sinkhole Tour of Centurion, akin to Hollywood's Grave Line Tours (Although being winter, Lourensa herself is not topless.)
We visit the Big Five sinkholes in Centurion, as ranked by the City of Tshwane. So far, only one sinkhole on the list is being under repairs.

Summary:
Centurion currently has 63 sinkholes.
The ground is dolomitic, and the suburb has many water leaks from ageing infrastructure. Summer rainstorms bring tension and anxiety to residents as the ground disappears beneath their feet.

Centurion Hospice, Unitas Hospital, businesses and private homes have been severely affected, not to mention motorists and pedestrians. Currently a bridge has been built in Clifton Rd that carries the Eskom lines, and the Rand Water pipeline and sewerage pipes. These are at risk as the hole gets bigger every month.

Lyttleton was originally a farm and should never have been developed into a town. It falls in the Transvaal Basin dolomite rock area. According to a geological map of Centurion, most of the suburb has a mid-level risk of developing a sinkhole, and a substantial portion is at high risk. More than 100 sinkholes had already been registered between 1970 and 2012 in Centurion’s business district alone. The tempo has since picked up.
There are no quick fixes for sinkholes. It’s expensive. (R2m each) In the past they closed sinkholes quite quickly, but now there are too many. The City of Tshwane wants Centurion to be declared a Disaster Area, and has appealed to the national government for a R200 million grant to repair the existing sinkholes

Apart from endangering lives, the sinkholes are affecting business operations, and the value of properties. Some residents are battling insurance companies to cover the damage. Some have sued the City Council.
Drilling of boreholes is banned; you cannot erect a carport/afdak without planning permission.
It’s one of the reasons why the Gautrain project was so expensive. They drilled right down into solid rock to ensure the line is stable. It can withstand a 20m sinkhole.


Further information:
Homeowners insurance does not cover sinkholes. This is a separate insurance that has to be added to your policy.

We visit three premises: a private home, a private business and the Centurion Hospice to hear how this problem has affected them




Extra Budget Items:
Party Bus: We need to hire the party bus from Centurion Limos for a couple of hours

Drone Pilot: We need drone footage of the various sinkholes, particularly in Clifton Avenue

Script:


LIVING ON CHEESE

V/O: Imagine waking up to find your gate two metres below your driveway. That’s the reality for some residents of Centurion outside Pretoria.

Tiddo: That’s the first one that fell. Obviously the second one is the one on the corner on the other side.

Lourensa: So, you are between two sinkholes?

Tiddo: So, we are on the island here.

Dorothy: That hole is where it started, and then it just became bigger and bigger.

Tertius: This one, it’s been here for nearly a year-and-a half now. The last sinkhole closest to us now fell two, three months ago in March.

V/O: Like a quarter of Gauteng province, Centurion is built on dolomite, the same rock that formed the Sterkfontein Caves over billions of years. The difference is - in Centurion they don’t know where the caves are.

Tiddo: So, you cross your fingers and hope it’s not going to happen.

Link: It’s quite difficult to see a sinkhole from ground level, and with 63 sinkholes in Centurion we decided we needed a higher vantage point.
So, join us as we set off on the great Centurion Sinkhole Safari.

V/O: We don’t have to travel far to spot the first one. The roads are closed; yellow barricades and hazard signs warn of the danger. There are so many sinkholes in the area the locals say they’re ‘living on cheese’ – like Swiss cheese.

Link: It’s well-known that Centurion is built on dolomite, in fact there’s so much of it they’ve been mining it for decades. Now dolomite dissolves in acidic liquids like stormwater, rainwater and sewerage. Which means a leaky pipe can spell disaster.

V/O: This is Centurion’s newest sinkhole, outside the Dutch Reformed Church in Lyttleton.

Wesley: So, what happened was, there was a leak; it was unfortunately not detected and when it was detected it was too late. The flange was leaking; it caused the secondary area to be dilapidated and collapsed onto a secondary piping which is the Rand Water pipe.

V/O: Wesley Jacobs represents the Freedom Front + in the Tshwane City Council.

Wesley: The crux of the matter is the dilapidation of the old asbestos piping, the old infrastructure. You know, for far too long the infrastructure of this particular area has been neglected. There’s been no upgrades for the last 70 years, let’s call it.

V/O: A report published in 1950 warns that sinkhole danger zones should be accurately identified when developing in dolomite areas like Pretoria.

V/O: But the warning was ignored, and Centurion was developed in the 1960’s. A recent map shows the high-risk areas in red, and the medium risk areas in yellow. The red dots on this map are all the sinkholes south of Pretoria.

Link: I’ve always heard about the sinkhole problem in Centurion, but it’s only when I stood 2 meters below the road that I really understood how bad it is. And for me, this is personal. My grandparents went to this Church. Their funerals were held here. And I can just imagine what they would say if they could see it now.

V/O: Research shows that 97% of Centurion sinkholes are caused by leaks. Just a block away from the Church is another one that formed 2 years ago. Tiddo Voogt shows us the asbestos pipe that caused the damage.

Tiddo: So how long was it leaking, I do not know, because you couldn’t see anything visually from the top.

Lourensa: How old are these pipes?

Tiddo: I don’t know, I’ve lived here 45 years; and as far as I know they have never replaced the pipes.

V/O: The sinkhole means there’s no proper drainage for the street, and in heavy downpours his garden is flooded.

Tiddo: All this water that comes down goes through my property.

Tiddo: “There you can see it all, onto the lawn.”

V/O: Gert Eloff owns two houses across the road that he rents out. Street access is blocked off by the sinkhole, and for two years they’ve had to use the neighbour’s driveway.

Lourensa: How much have you had to spend to ensure that your tenants can actually access the road?

Gert: Well, I have to put up a strong electric motor there, lay on electricity. I have to get 16 remote controls for the gates.

Lourensa: Do you think there’d be any way that you’d be able to sell this property again?

Gert: There’s no way you can sell it. Whoever will invest in the houses on the moment? It is impossible!

V/O: But that hasn’t stopped the City from increasing the market valuation of his properties by more than double this year.

Tertius: You know we pay rates and taxes here to the extent of R700 000 a year, just on property tax for this little 2000 square metre stand, and that’s the service that you get.

V/O: Tertius Zitzke is the CEO of 4Sight, a listed company with offices in Fourways and Centurion. When a water leak on the pavement caused a sinkhole in March, their boundary wall collapsed. As yet, there are no plans for repair.

Tertius: A senior city official wrote back to me that we must do an assessment by an engineer of the entire hole, and then they will look at it as well, and then assess, because they don’t have the staff that can do that. I mean an assessment like that costs R350 000 you know. We’ve got quotes for that.

Lourensa: And they expect you to do that?

Tertius: So, they expect us to do that and give them an assessment, and then what will happen? So, I got an email back saying we are – at that stage there were 40 in the area, 40 sinkholes – and we are, you are number 40.

V/O: This sinkhole is Number 13 on the City’s priority list. Lucky number 13 it seems, as it’s finally being repaired. After more than three years, people have learned to live with it.

Jaco: We don’t know what the caves look like underneath in the dolomite. So, they can be massive, they can be small, and this one is a little bit on the deeper side.

V/O: A drone shot reveals the cavernous depths beneath the road. Civil Engineer Jaco du Plessis explains that no two sinkholes are the same and they take time to be assessed.

Jaco: It takes quite a bit of money as well; sometimes you have to come with the drill to drill around it to determine where the cave is and how far the cave extends.

Lourensa: How much does it cost to fix an average sinkhole?

Jaco: I can’t give you an average cost; it’s almost impossible to say.
The one on the N1- they used 22400 cubic metres of concrete, so that’s R23 million – just concrete.

Lourensa: So, there’s no perfect solution to fixing a sinkhole?

Jaco: No. Preventing it is probably the better way, but it’s fairly difficult.

V/O: So, we go looking for possible solutions. On our journey, we find former Tshwane Mayor Cilliers Brink. He’s been called out by a concerned resident to inspect a stormwater drain.
Cilliers: So, you can hear this water. And you know there isn’t rain, so it isn’t stormwater. That’s a leak.

Lourensa: Do you have technology as a city to detect these leaks?

Cilliers: Yes; two years ago the City concluded a partnership with the Danish government, and as part of that partnership they’ve provided technology which uses sound waves – and I’m using ordinary language to describe this – there’s a more sophisticated way of doing so, but it tells you essentially where there are underground leaks and then you can dig it up and you can prevent pipes from collapsing completely, and you can stop leaks. It’s not just good for preventing sinkholes, it’s also good for saving money.

V/O: Next, we take a detour on our whistlestop tour to meet Nomvelo Mkhize, a geologist from the Council for Geoscience.

Nomvelo: So, the science is there, it’s existing, but obviously there needs to be investment into science to get to a point where we comfortably say that we have the necessary measures.

Lourensa: What are those measures?

Nomvelo: Like your basalt fibre pipes which we have seen around the world that can be a substitute, or that can work better in such areas. So, with the development of science and putting measures in place it can be mitigated.

V/O: Basalt fibre pipes are highly resistant to corrosion, even in acidic conditions. But too late for Centurion’s biggest sinkhole. When the ground gave way in 2022, so did the sewerage pipes, which played havoc with the neighbouring Hospice.

Dorothy: We had the sewerage come through the bathrooms and toilets, and it came through running from that side, and it came through this side as well; and all the sewerage – that grey, horrible, smelly, stinking sewerage – came through here.

Lourensa: Like a river?

Dorothy: Like a river ja.
And we had to remove the patients because you can’t have them in a situation like that.

V/O: Manager Dorothy Wye says the foul-smelling flood happened five times and led to the closure of the Hospice.

Dorothy: But the last one was so horrible, and municipality came and said they’re going to build the bridge with the pipes underneath; lift the pipes so it doesn’t run in here.

V/O: The bridge alone cost R6.5 million, but the sinkhole, which is 20m deep, is still growing. Neighbouring houses suffered structural damage and had to be abandoned.

Link: So now we’ve seen the Big Five, which means there are only 58 sinkholes to go. Now we can’t possibly get to them all in one day, but neither can the city. Because there’s no quick fix, and there’s not nearly enough money.

V/O: With a budget of only R15m for sinkhole repairs, it would take years just to repair this one.

MMC: But now that we’ve got a funded budget, we are going to be able to borrow money from various banks so that we can invest in replacing the water pipes and also investing in the sewer infrastructure.

V/O: Member of the Mayoral Committee Kholofelo Morodi has applied to national government to have Centurion declared a Disaster Area.

MMC: This is a disaster, and we need that help. And infrastructure – after years and years – it’s very difficult to expect the municipality on the budget that we have, to address 63 sinkholes; so, they need to do their part as well.

Lourensa: What will it cost to fix the sinkholes in Centurion?

MMC: So just doing the repairs to the sinkholes we worked out that we need R350 million.

Lourensa: And how much will it cost to address the pipes and water infrastructure?

MMC: Much more than that; we can’t even quantify at this stage.

Lourensa: So, for the residents that are desperate for answers about how long this will take, do you have a realistic answer?

MMC: It’s very difficult; what we do have in our control is the fact that we are going to make sure that we respond to water leaks timeously. We are also going to make sure that we go after the people that keep on drilling boreholes.

V/O: In winter there’s some respite, but when the rains come Centurion will be living on the edge.

Lourensa: How old are these pipes? Tiddo: I don’t know, I’ve lived here 45 years; and as far as I know they have never replaced the pipes. V/O: The sinkhole means there’s no proper drainage for the street, and in heavy downpours his garden is flooded. Tiddo: All this water that comes down goes through my property. Tiddo: “There you can see it all, onto the lawn.” V/O: Gert Eloff owns two houses across the road that he rents out. Street access is blocked off by the sinkhole, and for two years they’ve had to use the neighbour’s driveway. Lourensa: How much have you had to spend to ensure that your tenants can actually access the road? Gert: Well, I have to put up a strong electric motor there, lay on electricity. I have to get 16 remote controls for the gates. Lourensa: Do you think there’d be any way that you’d be able to sell this property again? Gert: There’s no way you can sell it. Whoever will invest in the houses on the moment? It is impossible! V/O: But that hasn’t stopped the City from increasing the market valuation of his properties by more than double this year. Tertius: You know we pay rates and taxes here to the extent of R700 000 a year, just on property tax for this little 2000 square metre stand, and that’s the service that you get. V/O: Tertius Zitzke is the CEO of 4Sight, a listed company with offices in Fourways and Centurion. When a water leak on the pavement caused a sinkhole in March, their boundary wall collapsed. As yet, there are no plans for repair. Tertius: A senior city official wrote back to me that we must do an assessment by an engineer of the entire hole, and then they will look at it as well, and then assess, because they don’t have the staff that can do that. I mean an assessment like that costs R350 000 you know. We’ve got quotes for that. Lourensa: And they expect you to do that? Tertius: So, they expect us to do that and give them an assessment, and then what will happen? So, I got an email back saying we are – at that stage there were 40 in the area, 40 sinkholes – and we are, you are number 40. V/O: This sinkhole is Number 13 on the City’s priority list. Lucky number 13 it seems, as it’s finally being repaired. After more than three years, people have learned to live with it. Jaco: We don’t know what the caves look like underneath in the dolomite. So, they can be massive, they can be small, and this one is a little bit on the deeper side. V/O: A drone shot reveals the cavernous depths beneath the road. Civil Engineer Jaco du Plessis explains that no two sinkholes are the same and they take time to be assessed. Jaco: It takes quite a bit of money as well; sometimes you have to come with the drill to drill around it to determine where the cave is and how far the cave extends. Lourensa: How much does it cost to fix an average sinkhole? Jaco: I can’t give you an average cost; it’s almost impossible to say. The one on the N1- they used 22400 cubic metres of concrete, so that’s R23 million – just concrete. Lourensa: So, there’s no perfect solution to fixing a sinkhole? Jaco: No. Preventing it is probably the better way, but it’s fairly difficult. V/O: So, we go looking for possible solutions. On our journey, we find former Tshwane Mayor Cilliers Brink. He’s been called out by a concerned resident to inspect a stormwater drain. Cilliers: So, you can hear this water. And you know there isn’t rain, so it isn’t stormwater. That’s a leak. Lourensa: Do you have technology as a city to detect these leaks? Cilliers: Yes; two years ago the City concluded a partnership with the Danish government, and as part of that partnership they’ve provided technology which uses sound waves – and I’m using ordinary language to describe this – there’s a more sophisticated way of doing so, but it tells you essentially where there are underground leaks and then you can dig it up and you can prevent pipes from collapsing completely, and you can stop leaks. It’s not just good for preventing sinkholes, it’s also good for saving money. V/O: Next, we take a detour on our whistlestop tour to meet Nomvelo Mkhize, a geologist from the Council for Geoscience. Nomvelo: So, the science is there, it’s existing, but obviously there needs to be investment into science to get to a point where we comfortably say that we have the necessary measures. Lourensa: What are those measures? Nomvelo: Like your basalt fibre pipes which we have seen around the world that can be a substitute, or that can work better in such areas. So, with the development of science and putting measures in place it can be mitigated. V/O: Basalt fibre pipes are highly resistant to corrosion, even in acidic conditions. But too late for Centurion’s biggest sinkhole. When the ground gave way in 2022, so did the sewerage pipes, which played havoc with the neighbouring Hospice. Dorothy: We had the sewerage come through the bathrooms and toilets, and it came through running from that side, and it came through this side as well; and all the sewerage – that grey, horrible, smelly, stinking sewerage – came through here. Lourensa: Like a river? Dorothy: Like a river ja. And we had to remove the patients because you can’t have them in a situation like that. V/O: Manager Dorothy Wye says the foul-smelling flood happened five times and led to the closure of the Hospice. Dorothy: But the last one was so horrible, and municipality came and said they’re going to build the bridge with the pipes underneath; lift the pipes so it doesn’t run in here. V/O: The bridge alone cost R6.5 million, but the sinkhole, which is 20m deep, is still growing. Neighbouring houses suffered structural damage and had to be abandoned. Link: So now we’ve seen the Big Five, which means there are only 58 sinkholes to go. Now we can’t possibly get to them all in one day, but neither can the city. Because there’s no quick fix, and there’s not nearly enough money. V/O: With a budget of only R15m for sinkhole repairs, it would take years just to repair this one. MMC: But now that we’ve got a funded budget, we are going to be able to borrow money from various banks so that we can invest in replacing the water pipes and also investing in the sewer infrastructure. V/O: Member of the Mayoral Committee Kholofelo Morodi has applied to national government to have Centurion declared a Disaster Area. MMC: This is a disaster, and we need that help. And infrastructure – after years and years – it’s very difficult to expect the municipality on the budget that we have, to address 63 sinkholes; so, they need to do their part as well. Lourensa: What will it cost to fix the sinkholes in Centurion? MMC: So just doing the repairs to the sinkholes we worked out that we need R350 million. Lourensa: And how much will it cost to address the pipes and water infrastructure? MMC: Much more than that; we can’t even quantify at this stage. Lourensa: So, for the residents that are desperate for answers about how long this will take, do you have a realistic answer? MMC: It’s very difficult; what we do have in our control is the fact that we are going to make sure that we respond to water leaks timeously. We are also going to make sure that we go after the people that keep on drilling boreholes. V/O: In winter there’s some respite, but when the rains come Centurion will be living on the edge.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Welcome to Centurion - where a water leak is not just a water leak - it literally dissolves the ground beneath your feet.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Lourensa takes us on a topless party bus Sinkhole Tour of Centurion, akin to Hollywood's Grave Line Tours (Although being winter, Lourensa herself is not topless.) We visit the Big Five sinkholes in Centurion, as ranked by the City of Tshwane. So far, only one sinkhole on the list is being under repairs.
metadata.Summary: Centurion currently has 63 sinkholes. The ground is dolomitic, and the suburb has many water leaks from ageing infrastructure. Summer rainstorms bring tension and anxiety to residents as the ground disappears beneath their feet. Centurion Hospice, Unitas Hospital, businesses and private homes have been severely affected, not to mention motorists and pedestrians. Currently a bridge has been built in Clifton Rd that carries the Eskom lines, and the Rand Water pipeline and sewerage pipes. These are at risk as the hole gets bigger every month. Lyttleton was originally a farm and should never have been developed into a town. It falls in the Transvaal Basin dolomite rock area. According to a geological map of Centurion, most of the suburb has a mid-level risk of developing a sinkhole, and a substantial portion is at high risk. More than 100 sinkholes had already been registered between 1970 and 2012 in Centurion’s business district alone. The tempo has since picked up. There are no quick fixes for sinkholes. It’s expensive. (R2m each) In the past they closed sinkholes quite quickly, but now there are too many. The City of Tshwane wants Centurion to be declared a Disaster Area, and has appealed to the national government for a R200 million grant to repair the existing sinkholes Apart from endangering lives, the sinkholes are affecting business operations, and the value of properties. Some residents are battling insurance companies to cover the damage. Some have sued the City Council. Drilling of boreholes is banned; you cannot erect a carport/afdak without planning permission. It’s one of the reasons why the Gautrain project was so expensive. They drilled right down into solid rock to ensure the line is stable. It can withstand a 20m sinkhole.
metadata.Further information: Homeowners insurance does not cover sinkholes. This is a separate insurance that has to be added to your policy. We visit three premises: a private home, a private business and the Centurion Hospice to hear how this problem has affected them
